concept.technique_name: context clue matching for two-blank text completion

examples.problem_statement: The film was (i) _________ (ii) _________ by critics; not a single reviewer had any positive thing to say about it. Blank (i): warily / mendaciously / roundly. Blank (ii): lauded / panned / venerated.

solution.operation: Read the clause after the semicolon: "not a single reviewer had any positive thing to say about it"
solution.result: The pair of blanks must together mean something like "unanimously criticized" or "100% disliked"
solution.description: Use the second half of the sentence as the clue: because no reviewer had anything positive to say, the film was completely and universally criticized, so set that meaning as the target both blanks must hit.

solution.operation: Test blank (i) against the target meaning: roundly = "emphatically", "so thoroughly as to leave no doubt"
solution.result: Roundly supplies the "unanimously / thoroughly" half of the target meaning
solution.description: Check the first blank, which must carry the totality of the criticism; roundly means emphatically or so thoroughly as to leave no doubt, which is exactly that sense.

solution.operation: Test blank (ii) against the target meaning: panned = "reviewed negatively", used almost always of plays, movies, etc.
solution.result: Panned supplies the "criticized" half and fits the film-review context
solution.description: Check the second blank, which must carry the negative-review sense; panned means reviewed negatively and is almost always used of plays and movies, making it a perfect match for a film judged by critics.

key_reminders: The clue for both blanks lives in the clause after the semicolon, not in the blanks themselves.
Roundly means emphatically or so thoroughly as to leave no doubt.
Panned means reviewed negatively and is used almost exclusively of plays, films, and similar performances.
common_mistakes: Choosing lauded or venerated for blank (ii), which reverse the polarity the "not a single positive thing" clue demands.
Choosing warily or mendaciously for blank (i), which describe the manner or honesty of the criticism rather than its thoroughness.

examples.problem_statement: X is the set of all integers n that satisfy the inequality 2 \le |n| \le 5. Quantity A: the absolute value of the greatest integer in X. Quantity B: the absolute value of the least integer in X. Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.

solution.result: A nonzero number and its negative have the same absolute value
solution.description: Record the fact the whole comparison rests on: taking absolute value erases sign, so a number and its negative are indistinguishable once the bars are applied.

solution.result: The positive integers 2, 3, 4, 5 and the negative integers -2, -3, -4, -5, and no others
solution.description: Because the condition is on |n|, test both signs at each magnitude from 2 through 5; every such integer qualifies and nothing outside that magnitude band does.

solution.result: The set X written out in increasing order
solution.description: Collect the qualifying integers into the set X and order them so the greatest and least members can be read straight off the ends.

solution.operation: Greatest element of X = 5, so Quantity A = |5|
solution.description: Take the rightmost member of X, which is 5, and apply the absolute value called for by Quantity A.

solution.operation: Least element of X = -5, so Quantity B = |-5|
solution.description: Take the leftmost member of X, which is -5, and apply the absolute value called for by Quantity B; by step 1 the minus sign drops away.

solution.result: Quantity A is equal to Quantity B
solution.description: Set the two computed values side by side; they are identical, so the two quantities are equal.

examples.answer: Choice C: The two quantities are equal.

key_reminders: An inequality stated on |n| admits both the positive and the negative integer of each qualifying magnitude.
"Greatest" and "least" refer to position on the number line, before any absolute value is taken.
common_mistakes: Reading 2 \le |n| \le 5 as 2 \le n \le 5 and building X from 2, 3, 4, 5 only, which makes the least element 2 and Quantity B appear smaller.
Calling -5 the "greatest in absolute value" and mixing up which endpoint feeds Quantity A versus Quantity B.

concept.technique_name: working backward through a doubling population chart

examples.problem_statement: Four years from now, the population of a colony of bees will reach 1.6 \times 10^8. If the population of the colony doubles every 2 years, what was the population 4 years ago? Options: 4 \times 10^7, 2 \times 10^7, 1 \times 10^7, 5 \times 10^6, 1 \times 10^6.

solution.operation: Build a population chart with rows at 4 years from now, 2 years from now, now, 2 years ago, 4 years ago
solution.result: A chart whose rows step by 2 years, matching the doubling interval
solution.description: Organize the given information into a chart whose rows advance in two-year jumps, because the doubling rate is once every two years, not every year.
Work backward one chart row by halving, since moving back two years undoes one doubling.
Step back another two years on the chart, halving the previous row to reach the present population.
Continue the same backward halving one more row to reach the population two years ago.
Halve once more to land on the target row, the population four years ago.
Convert the result to eliminate the decimal so it matches the form of the answer choices.

key_reminders: Doubling every 2 years means each chart row spans two years, not one.
Going backward in time undoes a doubling, so each backward row is a halving.
Scientific notation must be normalized before matching answer choices: 0.1 \times 10^8 = 1 \times 10^7.
common_mistakes: Halving once per year and taking eight halvings across the eight-year span instead of four.
Stopping at NOW (0.4 \times 10^8) or at 2 years ago (0.2 \times 10^8) instead of continuing to 4 years ago.
Leaving the answer as 0.1 \times 10^8 and failing to find it among the choices.
